paper.title: Over-Expression of LSD1 Promotes Proliferation, Migration and Invasion in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer

alerts.description: The publisher issued an expression of concern about this paper (notice 10.1371/journal.pone.0298436, 2024-02-02). Its reliability is in question, and it may later be corrected or retracted.

notice.title: Expression of Concern: Over-Expression of LSD1 Promotes Proliferation, Migration and Invasion in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
notice.text:
Expression of Concern: Over-Expression of LSD1 Promotes Proliferation, Migration and Invasion in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer

After this article [1] was published, the following issues were noted:

In Fig. 4, when levels are adjusted to visualize background, there appears to be a vertical discontinuity in the LSD1 panel between the 293T and A549 lanes.

The results shown in Fig. 7 do not correspond to the description in the Figure legend or the corresponding text of the Results section. Specifically, the figure does not report data for an LSD1 siRNA experiment and so the following result statement is not supported: “Compared with the control group, the number and rate of migrated cells was gradually reduced after transfection with LSD1 siRNA plasmid in the H460 cell lines.”

The article does not report sufficient detail about the controls used in the Flag-LSD1 and LSD1 siRNA transfection experiments to replicate these experiments.

Similarities were noted between this article [1] and work by other research groups which call into question the validity and provenance of the reported results.

The authors did not respond or could not be reached to discuss these issues.

The PLOS ONE Editors issue this Expression of Concern to inform readers of the unresolved issues.

draft_doc.title: Does LSD1 drive the migration of non-small cell lung cancer cells? A research plan
draft_doc.authors: N. Rahman and C. Ferreira · School of Biological Sciences, Fake Northern University
draft_doc.abstract: Most deaths from non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) follow spread of the tumour beyond the lung, yet the cell-intrinsic programmes that let tumour cells leave the primary site are only partly understood. Chromatin regulators that remove or add histone marks can switch whole sets of genes on or off, and several have been proposed as drivers of a migratory, mesenchymal state. This plan sets out a two-year project on one such regulator, the histone demethylase LSD1. Aim 1 will map LSD1 levels across a panel of authenticated NSCLC cell lines and relate them to baseline migration. Aim 2 will test whether lowering LSD1, by RNA interference, CRISPR interference and a small-molecule inhibitor, slows migration and invasion, and whether restoring LSD1 rescues the effect. Aim 3 will ask which genes LSD1 controls in migrating cells. The plan is pre-registered, uses blinded image analysis, and shares all raw images and code.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death, and non-small cell lung cancer accounts for most cases. Even among patients whose tumours are found early and removed completely, a substantial share later develop distant disease [10]. Metastasis begins with tumour cells that loosen their contacts with neighbours, move through the surrounding tissue and enter the circulation. Understanding which molecular switches make this possible is a prerequisite for therapies that would keep early-stage disease from spreading.
Over the last two decades it has become clear that the behaviour of a cancer cell is set not only by mutations in its DNA but also by how its chromatin is packaged. Histone proteins carry chemical marks, such as methyl and acetyl groups, that make neighbouring genes easier or harder to read. Enzymes that write and erase these marks therefore act as master regulators: changing one of them can shift the expression of hundreds of genes at once [2]. Methylation of lysine 4 on histone H3 is generally associated with active genes, and its loss from the promoters of epithelial genes has been described in lung tumours [20].
A recurring theme in this field is the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a programme in which epithelial cells lose adhesion molecules such as E-cadherin, gain mesenchymal markers such as N-cadherin and vimentin, and become more motile [6]. Several chromatin regulators have been reported to repress E-cadherin by modifying histones at its promoter [14], and EMT-like changes have been linked to invasion in carcinoma cells more broadly [3]. Whether a given regulator is a true driver of migration, rather than a marker that travels with it, can only be settled by experiments that change the regulator and measure the cells.
Those experiments are harder to interpret than they look. Knockdown by small interfering RNA can affect genes other than its target [8], cell lines drift or are misidentified [15], and wound-closure assays are sensitive to seeding density, scratch width and the analyst's choice of frames [1, 13]. A knockdown phenotype is most convincing when two independent methods agree and when restoring the target reverses it [9]. Our plan is built around these safeguards.
1.1 Scope of this plan
This document describes the rationale, the planned methods and the expected outcomes of a two-year project. It does not report new data. Section 2 summarises what is known about the enzyme we study, Section 3 explains why we think it controls migration, and Sections 4 to 6 set out the experiments, the analysis and the practical arrangements.

sections.heading: 2. Background: LSD1 and lung cancer
sections.text:
Lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1, also called KDM1A) removes methyl groups from mono- and dimethylated lysine 4 and lysine 9 of histone H3. Depending on the protein complex it joins, it can therefore either repress or activate transcription. LSD1 is required for normal development, and its activity can be blocked by monoamine oxidase inhibitors such as pargyline and by a growing family of more selective small molecules [7, 17]. This makes it attractive both as a tool to probe chromatin biology and as a possible drug target.
In the lung, the strongest clinical signal so far comes from tissue studies. In surgically resected samples from 80 NSCLC patients, Lv et al. found LSD1 expression higher in lung cancer tissue than in normal lung tissue, and over-expression of LSD1 protein was associated with shorter overall survival [12]. Associations of this kind are a reason to look at LSD1 more closely, but they cannot tell us whether LSD1 causes aggressive behaviour or simply marks tumours that are aggressive for other reasons. A tumour that has already undergone EMT may express more of many chromatin regulators at once [6].
In other carcinomas, LSD1 has been reported to sit in complexes that repress epithelial genes, and lowering it has been linked with a return of E-cadherin [14]. Whether the same holds in lung cancer cells, and whether the effect is large enough to change how far and how fast cells move, is the question this project addresses.

sections.heading: 3. Rationale for Aim 2: does lowering LSD1 slow migration?
sections.text:
The central hypothesis of this plan is that LSD1 activity is needed for NSCLC cells to migrate, so that lowering LSD1 slows migration and invasion. The main evidence behind this hypothesis is a single cell-line study. Lv et al. [12] reported that, in a scratch assay, the number and rate of migrated H460 cells was gradually reduced after transfection with an LSD1 siRNA plasmid compared with the control group, and that the number of migrated A549 cells increased after transfection with a Flag-LSD1 plasmid (their Figure 7). We take this knockdown result as the clearest indication that LSD1 is a driver, and not only a marker, of migration in lung cancer cells, and Aim 2 is designed to extend it.
Three gaps remain. First, the knockdown was done with one siRNA reagent in one cell line, so off-target effects cannot be excluded [8]. Second, no rescue experiment was reported, leaving open whether restoring LSD1 reverses the phenotype [9]. Third, scratch assays measure a mixture of migration and proliferation unless proliferation is blocked, and the readout depends on image analysis choices [1, 13]. Aim 2 addresses each of these gaps in turn.
3.1 Hypotheses
H1: Lowering LSD1 by either RNA interference or CRISPR interference reduces the rate of wound closure in H460 and at least two further NSCLC lines, with proliferation blocked by mitomycin C. H2: Re-expressing an siRNA-resistant LSD1 restores the rate of wound closure. H3: A selective LSD1 inhibitor reproduces the effect of knockdown at concentrations that do not reduce cell viability over 48 h. H4: Lowering LSD1 reduces invasion through a matrigel layer in a transwell assay [5].

sections.heading: 4. Planned methods
sections.text:
Cell lines. We will use H460, A549 and four further NSCLC lines obtained from a recognised repository, authenticated by short tandem repeat profiling at the start of the project and every six months, and tested monthly for mycoplasma [15]. Each line will be used within ten passages of thawing.
Lowering and restoring LSD1. Each line will receive two independent siRNAs against LSD1 and a non-targeting control, and, separately, a CRISPR interference construct with two guide RNAs [21]. Knockdown will be confirmed at the protein level by Western blot with full, uncropped membranes archived, and at the mRNA level by qRT-PCR. For rescue, an siRNA-resistant LSD1 complementary DNA, and a catalytically inactive mutant, will be expressed from an inducible vector. Every construct, sequence and control will be listed in a public protocol.
Migration and invasion. Wound closure will be measured in a 96-well format with a standard wound-making tool, imaged every two hours for 48 h, and quantified by a fixed, pre-registered pipeline [4, 19]. Invasion will be measured in matrigel-coated transwells at 24 h, counting cells on the lower surface in ten fields per insert [5]. Image analysis will be done blind to condition.
Statistics. The primary outcome is the relative wound density at 24 h. A difference of 15 percentage points between knockdown and control, with the variability seen in our pilot images, needs six biological replicates per condition for 90% power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05 [18]. Repeated measurements will be analysed with a mixed model with random effects for plate and experiment day [19]. The analysis plan will be registered before the first experiment [16].

sections.heading: 5. Expected results and alternatives
sections.text:
If LSD1 drives migration, we expect both knockdown methods to slow wound closure in most lines, the rescue construct to restore it, and the catalytically inactive mutant to fail to restore it. The inhibitor should reproduce the knockdown at non-toxic doses. In that case Aim 3 will compare gene expression in migrating cells with and without LSD1, with particular attention to E-cadherin and other EMT genes [6, 14].
If only one knockdown method slows migration, or the rescue fails, the most likely explanation is an off-target effect, and we will report the result as evidence against a general role for LSD1 in migration. If knockdown slows migration in some lines but not others, we will relate the effect to baseline LSD1 levels measured in Aim 1. A null result in all lines would argue that the association of LSD1 with poor outcome in patients reflects something other than a direct effect on migration, and we will say so.
We will publish all results, positive or negative, together with the raw images, the analysis code and the registered plan [16, 22]. Image integrity will be checked before submission with the screening tools now used by many journals [11].

sections.heading: 6. Timeline, resources and data management
sections.text:
Months 1 to 6: cell line authentication, construct validation and the pilot imaging needed to fix the analysis pipeline. Months 7 to 15: Aim 1 and the knockdown and rescue experiments of Aim 2. Months 13 to 20: inhibitor and invasion experiments. Months 18 to 24: Aim 3, analysis and writing.
The project needs one postdoctoral researcher and half of a technician's time, access to the institutional live-cell imaging system, and consumables for about 1,400 imaged wells. All raw images will be deposited in a public image repository under an open licence within six months of the end of each aim, and the analysis code will be versioned in a public code repository from the first day [22].
The main risk is that knockdown of LSD1 slows proliferation enough to confound migration. Blocking proliferation during the assay, and measuring viability in parallel, is intended to separate the two. A second risk is that the effect is smaller than expected; the power calculation is based on a conservative difference, and the mixed model uses all time points.

must_include: says the expression of concern states that Fig. 7 does not show LSD1 siRNA data, so the H460 knockdown migration result is not supported
says the draft's Aim 2 rationale rests on that H460 siRNA migration result
advises not resting Aim 2 on this result alone, for example by hedging the wording, adding independent evidence, or presenting the effect as what the planned experiments will test
notes that the concern is unresolved (the authors did not respond) and the paper may later be corrected or retracted
must_not_include: says the draft's use of the migration result is not affected by the concern

expected.why: Expression of concern about data and results = medium (rubric); the notice is about this paper. Its scope is specific parts (Figs 4 and 7, the transfection controls), though "Similarities were noted between this article [1] and work by other research groups which call into question the validity and provenance of the reported results." can be read as the whole paper, so both scopes are accepted. The draft's Section 3 rests its central hypothesis on the H460 siRNA migration result, which is the exact statement the notice withdraws support for: "The results shown in Fig. 7 do not correspond to the description in the Figure legend or the corresponding text of the Results section." and "Specifically, the figure does not report data for an LSD1 siRNA experiment and so the following result statement is not supported". So that use is key_evidence and affected: key_evidence x medium = medium. The Section 2 survival sentence is a background use; it can be affected or unclear, but at most low. The concern is open: "The authors did not respond or could not be reached to discuss these issues." and "The PLOS ONE Editors issue this Expression of Concern to inform readers of the unresolved issues." Saying retracted, or high, is overreach; none or unaffected misses the notice quoting the draft's own claim.
